QSR Daily Demand

Stage 1: from sales patterns to practical decisions

Student Analyst

The business question

Where does demand concentrate, when does it change, and which relationships deserve attention?

  • One selected restaurant: R07, Minneapolis
  • Daily item-level sales, 2021–2025
  • Descriptive analysis using the concepts covered in Weeks 1–5

What sells?

  • Drinks lead total recorded units.
  • Soft Drink Regular, French Fries Regular, and Classic Cheeseburger are among the leading individual items.
  • Category and item rankings help focus stock checks.

Business implication: Start operational planning with the products that account for much of the recorded volume.

When does demand change?

  • Average daily demand is strongest in Jul and lowest in Jan.
  • Category-specific monthly lines help show whether every menu group follows the same pattern.
  • Weekday boxplots add the variation hidden by averages.

Business implication: Use historical demand as a starting point for staffing and preparation—not as a guarantee for a particular day.

What relationships did we examine?

  • A correlation heatmap and follow-up scatterplot compare daily patterns for high-volume products.
  • Violin/boxplots compare promotional and non-promotional distributions by category.
  • Scatterplots test price and preparation time against average item-day quantity.
  • Faceted temperature plots and event comparisons add external context.

Interpretation: Correlation does not prove causation. Product co-movement is not proof of same-transaction purchases.

Volume is not value

  • Drinks lead units.
  • Burgers lead estimated total food-cost margin, followed by Combos and Chicken.
  • The estimate uses listed price and food cost across the full history; it is not net profit.

Business implication: Consider demand and unit economics together.

What should happen next?

  1. Protect availability of core items.
  2. Plan for seasonal and weekday variation.
  3. Evaluate promotions by category and compare like with like.
  4. Prepare for specific local events.
  5. Use follow-up tests before attributing changes to advertising or weather.

Note

Stage 1 ends with descriptive analysis and business recommendations. No machine-learning model is included.

Stage 2: from describing demand to predicting it

First analysis (Stage 1): what happened. Updated analysis (Stage 2): what can we predict, and how wrong might we be?

  • Stage 2 adds Weeks 8-12: modeling, predictions, and assessment on the same R07 daily data
  • Numbers on these slides are from the rendered Modeling page, Nov 22, 2026, not typed from a plan

Week 15 structure: first show what Stage 1 described, then show what Stage 2 changed.

Week 8: my first model, and the split-first rule

  • Target: total daily demand for R07, one row per date, a regression problem
  • Split first: 1,460 training days / 366 test days, with a seed, before any preprocessing
  • Recipe v1 (lean): median imputation for numbers, dummies for weekday and month, no normalization for a plain linear model
  • The recipe is prepped inside the workflow on training data only, so the test set does not leak into the fit

The biggest Week 8 lesson: the recipe is prepped inside the workflow on training data only, or the test set leaks.

Week 10: predictions, judged against baselines

  • Every model predicts the same held-out test days
  • Two baselines predicted too: overall mean (test RMSE 428.0) and weekday average (test RMSE 383.0)
  • The winner beats both by a wide margin: test RMSE 130.7, against 383.0 for the weekday baseline
  • Predicted-vs-actual and residuals-over-time charts on the Modeling page show where the model fails, not just how much

A model that cannot beat the weekday average has learned nothing. The baselines keep the results honest.

Weeks 11-12: assessment before recommendation

One ranked table: test RMSE and MAE, 5-fold CV RMSE, and a time split (train 2021-2024, test 2025). Only the lasso penalty was tuned, on the folds, never on the test set.

Model Test RMSE Test MAE CV RMSE Time-test RMSE
LM + Recipe v2 130.7 84.8 110.6 134.2
Lasso + Recipe v2 130.8 85.0 110.8 134.1
Ridge + Recipe v2 137.8 89.8 116.1 137.8
Tree + Recipe v2 192.7 140.7 183.2 178.8
LM + Recipe v1 196.3 114.0 166.4 169.6
Weekday average 383.0 - - 373.1
Overall mean 428.0 - - 407.4

Winner: LM + Recipe v2 - test RMSE 130.7, MAE 84.8 units per day, R-squared 0.908 (time-test R-squared 0.924). Recipe v2, with season, events, precipitation type, and normalization, clearly beat the lean recipe, and the ranking holds across test, CV, and the time split.

Weeks 11-12 changed my order of work: metrics first, interpretation second, recommendation last. Lasso essentially ties LM on the time split, 134.1 against 134.2.

What I learned, in one slide

  • First analysis (Stage 1): describe honestly, keep the unit of observation straight, report negative results
  • Updated analysis (Stage 2): split first, compare against baselines, assess three ways before recommending
  • The course moved me from “what happened” to “what can we predict, and how wrong might we be” - and to saying the second part out loud
  • Next step if I continued: item-level promotion data and real weather forecasts as predictors

The course moved me from what happened to what we can predict, and how wrong we might be, and to saying the second part out loud.
